verdicts.reason:
The finding stands, with one narrowing. Two places are plainly wrong or misleading against the standard.

1. The I-SV-3B index table row (line 291) says "the checks drain in the check phase". Nothing can drain in check_phase. It is a bottom-up function phase, and when run_phase ends, its remaining task threads are killed. That makes it S1.
2. The "Expert: stopping at the goal without losing checks" section (line 602) and its SequenceDiagram (lines 625-640) teach a bare objection drop as the safe way to stop. That section's first bullet describes a pipelined DUT whose last results are still in flight, but nothing here holds the phase open. The diagram goes straight from "phase.drop_objection(this)" to "run_phase ends" and then check_phase. This contradicts the owning lesson. I-UVM-1C line 259 says a drop at the last stimulus "usually ends the phase too early". Its symptom table (line 429) says "The phase ended at the drop, and the response threads were killed" and gives the fix: phase_ready_to_end or a drain time. I-UVM-3C's "drain time 0" row shows the same loss (MON_INFLIGHT, matches=15 instead of 16).

The narrowing: the second sentence on line 602, taken alone, is literally true, because end-of-test checks do run in check_phase. The defect is what the section leaves out given its "without losing checks" heading. The interview option on line 683 ("drop the objection, so the scoreboard drains") is vague rather than false, but it repeats the same implication. The closure-workflow caption at line 398 ("drops its objection so the run phase can end") is accurate. Adding the drain there is S3 polish, not part of the defect.

Within the same lesson, coverage-apis.mdx gets it right: step 6, line 615, says "let the checker drain ... then $finish ... (in UVM, drop the objection)". That shows the index page is the outlier.

The proposed fix agrees with the standard. Drain time is §10.5.1.3.7, the clause I-UVM-1C and I-UVM-3C already cite. A raise and drop of an objection during phase_ready_to_end starts a new iteration of the callback (§9.3.1.3.3, which points to 13.1.4.3.2). So a scoreboard that raises in phase_ready_to_end and drops when pending reaches 0 is the mechanism the standard supports.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds, and it covers a little more than it says. The owning lesson, A-UVM-5, lists "Callbacks run in registration order" as a misconception (line 559, and flashcard a-uvm-5-6 says "not registration order"). A-UVM-9:1853 and E-DBG-1:784 state the same thing as fact for report catchers. Those two lessons are right. The standard defines add() order in terms of earlier adds: under the default UVM_APPEND a callback runs "after previously added callbacks", and under UVM_PREPEND "ahead of previously added callbacks" (§10.7.2.3.1).

A-UVM-5's reason is also wrong. In uvm-core, the first instance add() copies the type-wide queue in its existing order and then pushes the new callback. A later type-wide add() pushes onto the type-wide queue and onto every existing instance queue, at the back for APPEND. So with only UVM_APPEND, each object's queue is always in add order. Only UVM_PREPEND, or a delete followed by a re-add, moves a callback out of that order. A-UVM-5's own step table (lines 318-334) and line 325 show exactly this, so the misconception row contradicts its own lesson as well.

The same claim appears in two more places the finding does not list: the A-UVM-5 stage figure (aria-label at line 594, and the "trap: type-wide copy, PREPEND, later type-wide adds" text at line 603). They need the same fix.

All the facts check out against the source:

IEEE 1801 is not in the sources folder, so I cannot check the finding's claim that §6.5 and §6.7 leave states and transitions to the user. I could check the SystemVerilog side (illegal transition bins, §19.5.6), and the E-PWR-1 code says what the finding says. This is a modelling disagreement between the two lessons, not a fact one of them gets wrong against a standard, so S2 is the right severity.

Three of the finding's claims stand:
(a) I-SV-8 draws OFF to RUN as a legal arrow ("power on, reset, release"). E-PWR-1 makes PD_OFF => PD_RUN an illegal bin, and neither lesson maps one set of states onto the other.
(b) I-SV-8's legal cold wake (RUN to OFF to RUN, "everything at reset values; no restore expected") would fail E-PWR-1's a_release_after_wake. I traced the flag logic. Power loss clears restored and sets ever_off. The reset that follows clears restored again, because ever_off is 1. No restore comes, so at the release restored is 0 and the assertion fires. E-PWR-1 also states the rule in general terms: "after a power loss the release is legal only after power, then reset, then restore".
(c) I-SV-8 lines 512 and 597 promise that E-PWR-1 "covers every state and arrow". E-PWR-1 covers only its own three derived states plus the full retention cycle and the light sleep (Kata 2). It has nothing for I-SV-8's RET-versus-OFF difference, for RET to OFF, for the illegal OFF to RET negative test, or for a cold wake.

One claim needs narrowing. "E-PWR-1's PD_OFF is I-SV-8's RET" is not accurate. PD_OFF only means "the switch has acknowledged power-off", and E-PWR-1 never models the retention supply. So PD_OFF stands for both of I-SV-8's RET and OFF. The fix's mapping table must say that.

The rest of the fix is consistent with the code. Under E-PWR-1's own derivation, a cold wake does go PD_OFF => PD_PARKED => PD_RUN, so it never hits the illegal bin. It is a_release_after_wake that rejects it.

The real problem is that the two lessons use the same words, OFF and RUN, for different states of the same PD_CPU, and neither gives a mapping.

1. **A promise E-PWR-1 does not keep.** I-SV-8 hands "these checks and the coverage" to E-PWR-1, and its VisualRecap says E-PWR-1 "covers every state and arrow". E-PWR-1 never separates RET from OFF. It has no cold wake (power on, reset, release with no restore), no RET to OFF, and no negative test for OFF to RET.
2. **A general rule that would fail a legal scenario.** E-PWR-1 states "after a power loss the release is legal only after power, then reset, then restore". Its checker clears `restored` on every power loss and on every reset once `ever_off` is 1. A cold wake, which I-SV-8 lists as legal with "no restore expected", would therefore fail `a_release_after_wake`. This only holds for a domain whose retention supply never switches off, and E-PWR-1 never says so. Its one mention, "The retention supply itself switched off loses the saved value too", does not link to I-SV-8's deep-off scenario.
3. **Same state names, different meanings.** OFF and RUN mean different things in the two lessons, with no mapping between them.

This is a planned spiral: E-PWR-1 links back to I-SV-8 at lines 19, 40 and 110. So it is not a duplicate topic, and none of the fixes below removes content.

The proposed fix is mostly safe. One part is not: adding a cold-wake variant that changes the checker code would also force changes to the logged 405 ns runs, the Predict answers, the troubleshooting table and the lab's PASS=5 target. Leave the code alone and change the prose instead.

verdicts.reason: The finding stands, in a narrower form. Two things hold up against the sources. (1) E-EMU-1 calls reversing the C field order "the portable fix", and IEEE 1800-2023 does not support that. Annex H.7.7 only says that element 0 of the svBitVecVal array holds the 32 least significant bits. It says nothing about how a C struct lies over that array. In the reversed struct {unsigned value; unsigned char idNum;}, value maps onto element 0 on any host where unsigned is 32 bits. But idNum is the first byte at offset 4. That byte holds idNum (the low 8 bits of element 1) only on a little-endian host. On a big-endian host it is the top byte of element 1, which is one of the unused bits whose contents are "undetermined". So the trick depends on the host's byte order and on the C ABI. It is not portable. Only the per-field bit-position methods are host-independent: shifts and masks, or svGetPartselBit/svPutPartselBit (both are real svdpi functions, H.11.5). (2) Both lessons teach the packed-struct-over-DPI layout trap in full, each with its own traced example and fix, and neither links to the other's section. The only links between the two lessons are the generic SCE-MI mention at E-UVM-ML-1 line 101 and the related-lesson lists (E-UVM-ML-1 line 1320, E-EMU-1 line 1682). I-SV-7 teaches the canonical form (line 486) but not the C-struct overlay trap, so neither topic owner covers it. One narrowing: the finding says E-UVM-ML-1 teaches "never rely on C layout". It does not say "never". It gives shift-and-mask as "the rule". So the lessons disagree on which fix to use, not on a stated fact, and the factual error is E-EMU-1's word "portable". verdicts.reason: This is not a §1.3 breach and not an S2. §1.3 is about topic ownership: one lesson teaches a topic in full, and other lessons link back instead of teaching it again. The capstone does not teach coherency again. It only asks the learner to plan around it in one template row ("DMA coherency": descriptor type x cache state x completion path) and in a few model-solution lines. So there is no duplicate. The topic is also not used before it is taught. B-AMBA-F2 is a core T3 module, so a learner on the core path (plan §1.1) has already worked through ACE line states and the coherency checker before reaching E-SOC-1 in T4. The lab also does not promise anything that no lesson teaches. What remains is a missing back-link from the capstone to B-AMBA-F2. That is "a link that would help", which is S3 and out of scope for round 2. One small aggravating fact: E-SOC-1's manifest prerequisites (A-UVM-8, A-UVM-4B, E-DBG-1) do not list B-AMBA-F2. A learner who jumps in by prerequisites alone could therefore miss it, but the core-path order still covers it. Of the two proposed fixes, adding a link is safe. Dropping the coherency row and the model-solution lines would be unsafe: it would cut correct content and leave README line 9 ("Two coherent CPU clusters") and line 13 ("AXI/ACE-capable interconnect") describing a design whose coherency nobody plans. If the lead wants the S3 fix anyway, add a B-AMBA-F2 link to the capstone README scenario and beside the template's DMA coherency row, and add B-AMBA-F2 to E-SOC-1's Related list. Leave the bug-class list as it is.
